1:
The single line that opens the chapter — But Job answered — carries, the witnesses agree, a startling change of tone, for the sufferer meets Bildad's short speech not with a groan but with a laugh. The reformed John Gill marvels that a man in Job's circumstances should have so much keenness of spirit, dealing in so much irony and mastering so much satire that he is able to laugh at his antagonist outright. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry is struck by the same thing: one would not have thought that Job, in so much pain and misery, could banter his friend as he does here and make himself merry with the impertinency of the discourse. Bildad, Henry says, thought he had made a fine speech, the matter so weighty and the language so fine that he had earned the double reputation of an oracle and an orator; Job peevishly enough shows that the performance was not so valuable as its author supposed, and ridicules him for it.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott explains why Job spends so little breath on the substance of it. Job himself had virtually said much the same as Bildad already, in ch. 9:2 and 14:4, granting that no man can be just with God nor bring a clean thing out of an unclean; so he makes no further comment on those remarks, but merely asks how Bildad has helped him thereby, or helped any other in a weak and helpless condition. The retort is not a denial of Bildad's doctrine but a dismissal of its usefulness.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the whole answer as the reproof of a man who has watched his opponents run out of arguments. Perceiving that his friends could no longer support their case on the ground they had assumed, Job sharply rebukes them for their want both of wisdom and of feeling in the first four verses, and then — as if to show how the theme ought to be handled — goes on to display the power and wisdom of God in the works of creation and providence, giving several proofs and adding at the last that even these are but a small specimen of an infinite skill and an unlimited power. The witnesses do not divide; they hear in the bare But Job answered the opening of a reply that sets the sharpest mockery and the loftiest praise the book has yet reached side by side.
2:
The mockery takes the form of a question Job will strike in three keys — how hast thou helped him that is without power? — and the witnesses divide over who this powerless one is. The reformed John Gill reads the whole verse of God, turning it, "whom hast thou helped? God?" A fine advocate Bildad has proved, representing the Almighty as though he were without power and could not help himself, as though he had no arm and needed one raised up in his behalf, as though he wanted wisdom and a counsellor — when he is God omnipotent, whose arm is strong and mighty and like none other, the all-wise God who never consults with his creatures nor admits them to his council. To suppose that such a Being's very essence had been copiously and plentifully declared in Bildad's few words is, Gill says, the height of arrogance and folly.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears instead a species of irony aimed at the friends' feebleness: "How wonderfully hast thou counselled the unskilful and strengthened the weak! Alas for you! ye could not give what ye did not possess." He sets beside it the Chaldee paraphrase, which keeps the same edge — "Why hast thou pretended to give succour, when thou art without strength? and save, while thy arm is weak? Why hast thou given counsel, when thou art without understanding?" On this reading the powerless one is Job himself, or any afflicted man to whom Bildad's barren comfort brought no strength at all.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers both senses into his cui bono — what good has all this done? Job would convince Bildad that he had done God no service and made him in no way beholden to him; for though it is our duty and honour to speak on God's behalf, we must not think he needs our service, nor will he accept it when it comes from a spirit of contention and contradiction rather than a sincere regard to his glory. So the difference is real, though the schools are not far apart: is the one "without power" the God whom Bildad officiously defends as though heaven needed an advocate, as Gill takes it, or the broken sufferer whom his counsel wholly failed to strengthen, as Clarke and the drift of the passage suggest? Either way the witnesses agree that Bildad has spent his eloquence to no purpose, helping neither the God who needs no help nor the man who needed it and found none.
3:
The taunt runs on into a second clause, how hast thou counselled him that hath no wisdom?, and the reformed John Gill lets Job grant the premise only to turn it. A man deprived of wisdom, Gill allows, has need of counsel, and it should be given him, and he does well both to ask and to take it. So suppose that I am the foolish, unwise creature you take me to be — what counsel and advice have you actually given me? what a wise counsellor have you shown yourself to be, or rather, what a miserable part have you acted under that character? The irony is that Bildad, having come to instruct a fool, has proved the poorer teacher of the two, offering nothing that a man in Job's straits could either use or trust.

On the closing words, how hast thou plentifully declared the thing as it is?, the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott offers a quiet correction of the rendering: the Hebrew, he says, is better given "How hast thou plentifully declared sound knowledge?" — so that Job is not merely mocking Bildad's clarity but bantering his conceit of having poured out a fulness of solid wisdom in a handful of words.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry catches the same self-satisfaction and exposes the vanity beneath it. Bildad was fond, as we are all apt to be, of his own notions, and thought them the only true and intelligible ones; he supposed he had declared the thing as it is, and declared it fully. But when we speak of the glory of God, Henry answers, we cannot declare the thing as it is, for here we see it through a glass darkly and cannot so much as order our speech concerning him by reason of darkness, as Job will own in ch. 37:19. And Bildad had spoken not fully but scantily, poorly, in comparison with the vast compass and copiousness of the subject. Henry adds the shrewd observation that Bildad thought his fellow-disputants mightily beholden to him for helping them, at a dead lift, to make good their part against Job when they were quite at a loss; for even weak disputants, when they grow warm, are apt to think truth more beholden to them than it really is. The witnesses do not divide; they read the verse as Job's mock-tribute to a counsellor who has counselled nothing, and a declarer who, thinking he had said all, has scarcely touched the fringe of his theme.
4:
"To whom hast thou uttered words? and whose spirit came from thee?" — the double question closes Job's reproof and, on one reading, quietly announces the strange thing he is about to do. The reformed John Gill takes the first half as wounded dignity and pastoral reproach at once: does Bildad imagine he is talking to an ignorant man, when Job knows as much of the Divine Being, his glories and his wondrous ways, as his friend does, or more? and does he weigh the circumstances of the man he addresses — one under great affliction, to whom it is unsuitable to press the greatness and majesty, the purity and strict justice of God, when it would have been far more proper and friendly to discourse of his loving-kindness and compassion, his readiness to forgive, and of the promised Redeemer, his righteousness and sacrifice?

The wesleyan-arminian voices sharpen the second question into a charge of plagiarism. Adam Clarke follows Mr. Good's rendering — "From whom hast thou pillaged speeches? and whose spirit hath issued forth from thee?" — and concurs with Dr. Stock in reading all that follows as a sample, ironically exhibited by Job, of the very harangues on the power and greatness of God which his friends had taken out of other men's mouths to deck their speeches with a borrowed lustre; only Job, descanting on the same theme, shows how far he can outgo them in eloquence and sublimity. Whatever spirit breathed in them, Clarke adds, it was not the Spirit of God, for in their answers falsehood was found. John Wesley keeps it plainer: for whose instruction were these things uttered — for mine, who know what the meanest persons are not ignorant of, that God is incomparably greater and better than his creatures? and who inspired thee with this profound discourse of thine?

The other grammatical-historical witness, Charles Ellicott, hears Job ask whether the words were not addressed to one who had said the very same himself — was it not my own breath, my own teaching, that came forth from you? — and then notes the turn the chapter takes, as Job sets out to show that it is not only the starry heavens that declare the glory of God, but the under-world likewise, and the universe at large. So a real difference of frame opens here: whether the sublime hymn that follows is Job's own adoring praise or, with Clarke and Stock, an ironic parody that beats the friends at their own borrowed eloquence. The witnesses do not divide over the sting of the question, only over the spirit of the verses it introduces.
5:
With the reproof done, Job plunges into the depths, and the very first word of his hymn — the Hebrew Rephaim, rendered "dead things" — sets the witnesses at variance. The reformed John Gill takes them for lifeless, inanimate things formed under the waters: grains of corn, which die before they are quickened and cannot grow without rain; or the metals and minerals, the pearls and corals and sea-plants, that men draw up from beneath the flood, following Aben Ezra and Ben Gersom. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley allows that same sense — amber, pearl, coral, and the ores brought forth from under the sea, whose waters, though higher than the earth, do not overwhelm it — but adds a darker alternative: that the word may mean dead men, and the worst of them, who mourn and groan from under the waters in their infernal habitations, forced at last to acknowledge the power they had despised.

That second reading the grammatical-historical witnesses press home. Charles Ellicott identifies the Rephaim as the old aboriginal race about the Dead Sea, a name that came to stand for the dead and the whole nether world; and he renders "are formed" rather "are pierced" or "tremble" — pierced through with terror — so that all the secrets of that invisible, undiscoverable world lie naked before God. Keil and Delitzsch hear the same note: the marrowless, bloodless shades below writhe like a woman in travail whenever the majesty of the heavenly Ruler is felt among them, as by the raging of the sea or the quaking of the earth.

A third reading turns on the giants. Adam Clarke denies that Rephaim means "dead things" at all, marshalling the versions — the Vulgate's "the giants groan from under the waters," the Septuagint's "are the giants formed," the Syriac and Arabic's "the giants are slain and drawn out of the water" — and refers the word to the antediluvians, the nephilim of Gen. 6:4, overwhelmed in the deluge, though he will also entertain the sea-monsters, the sharks and whales of the deep. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry joins the two, taking the giants both for the vast sea-creatures Bishop Patrick thought of and, with Joseph Mede, for the drowned giants of the old world, whose ruin typifies hell laid naked before God. So the debate stands genuinely open — inanimate treasures of the deep, the trembling shades of the dead, or the buried giants of a former world — and the witnesses agree only in this, that Job's point is the reach of God's dominion into a region utterly hidden from the eye of man.
6:
"Hell is naked before him, and destruction hath no covering" — Job carries the divine gaze one step lower, into the region man cannot see at all, and the witnesses trace the several senses of the words. The reformed John Gill lets "hell" bear its full range. It may be the place of the damned, hidden from men, yet wholly known to God, who made and ordained it, knows who are there and what torments they endure; or it may be Hades, the invisible world of departed spirits; or simply the grave — and in every sense it is naked and open to the eye of God. Beside him the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the whole movement in view: Bildad had extolled God's rule in the heights of heaven, his immediate surrounding, and Job now celebrates its extension to the very depths, so that neither the sea nor the realm of shades forms any barrier between God and what lies beneath — Sheol is bare before him, and the abyss has no covering.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fills in the ancient geography of the words. Sheol is the place of the dead, and Abaddon the place of the destroyer, where destruction reigns; the ancients imagined hell a vast gulf at the very centre of the earth, and Clarke quotes Virgil's picture of Tartarus sinking as far below the earth as heaven stands above it, where the Titan race, struck by the burning bolts, roll bellowing in the depths. Yet he is careful to add that the sacred writers would not countenance an opinion with nothing in fact to support it, however freely a poet might avail himself of a popular belief.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the comfort out of the terror. By hell and destruction we may understand the grave and those buried in it, who, though laid out of our sight, are still under the eye of God — which may strengthen our faith in the resurrection, for God knows where to find and whence to fetch all the scattered atoms of the consumed body. Or we may take them of the place of the damned, that hell and destruction which are said to be always before the Lord in Prov. 15:11. John Wesley reduces it to a sentence: hell itself, that place of utter darkness, is not hid from his sight, but lies open in his presence and under his providence. The witnesses do not divide; whether the word points to the grave, the unseen world, or the pit of the lost, they agree that nothing beneath is screened from the God whose dominion Job is exalting.
7:
Now comes the line the witnesses handle with the most wonder — that God stretcheth out the north over the empty place, and hangeth the earth upon nothing. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry dwells on the marvel of it: the vast terraqueous globe rests upon no pillars and hangs upon no axle-tree, yet by almighty power is firmly fixed and poised by its own weight — ponderibus librata suis, as the poet has it, upheld by the word of God's power, as the apostle says. The art of man, Henry observes, could not hang so much as a feather upon nothing, and yet the divine wisdom hangs the whole earth so; and the north he stretches over the empty place as at the first he stretched out the heavens like a curtain in Ps. 104:2.

On "the north" the grammatical-historical witnesses differ from some of their own school. Keil and Delitzsch reject the view of Hirzel, Ewald, and others that the word means the northern part of the earth, since the verb "stretcheth out" is used always of the heavens and never of the earth, and one expects the sky to be named alongside the earth; so they take it of the northern sky, spread over the void. John Wesley agrees, reading "the north" as the northern quarter of the heavens, put for the whole visible heaven because Job and his friends lived in a northern climate; and the earth hangs, he says, upon no props or pillars but God's own power and providence. The reformed John Gill likewise thinks of the northern hemisphere expanded over emptiness.

The great second clause draws out the boldest comment. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke notes that "the empty place" is al tohu, the hollow waste, the very word for the earth "without form" in Gen. 1:2, and records the Chaldee's cautious softening, "he lays the earth upon the waters, nothing sustaining it." But it is Charles Ellicott who states the astonishment plainly: if the words mean what they seem to — and it is hard to see what else they can mean — they furnish a very remarkable anticipation of the discoveries of science, Job describing more than three thousand years ago, in language of scientific accuracy, the condition of our globe and holding it forth as a proof of divine power. He notes that some have tried to explain the second clause of the destitution caused by famine, but that the terms of the first clause preclude it. The witnesses do not divide over the grandeur; they agree that in this one verse Job has said something truer of the earth than the science of his age could have taught him, and has said it to the glory of God.
8:
From the poised earth Job lifts his eye to the clouds, where God bindeth up the waters in his thick clouds, and the cloud is not rent under them. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry finds the wonder in the restraint: God binds the waters up as if they were tied fast in a bag, laid by till there is occasion to use them, and for all the vast weight of water so raised and stored, the cloud is not rent — for if it burst it would pour out like a spout and drown the ground; instead the waters distil through it drop by drop, in mercy to the earth, in small rain or great as he pleases. The reformed John Gill dwells on the same paradox: the clouds are of God's making, the exhaled vapours gathered into his chariots, and though they are but thin in themselves it is the more marvellous that so heavy a body of water should be held bound within them, as a thing tied up in a sack or in the skirt of a man's coat.

The grammatical-historical witnesses turn the marvel toward law. Keil and Delitzsch say that the clouds are masses of water rolled together which, suddenly set free, would deluge the ground, but the omnipotence of God holds them together so that they do not burst asunder under their burden — meaning, in plain terms, that the physical and meteorological laws of rain are of God's appointment. Charles Ellicott sets the picture beside the waters divided in Gen. 1:7: a vast treasury of water above the visible sky, kept there in apparent defiance of what we know as the laws of gravitation, and which all experience would say must fall of itself.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke supplies the mechanism the others leave implied. God drives together the aqueous particles raised by evaporation, so that, being condensed, they form the clouds that float in the atmosphere until, meeting with strong currents of wind or by the agency of the electric fluid, they are condensed still further, grow too heavy to be sustained, and fall as rain — and then, in Job's poetic language, the cloud is rent under them. The witnesses do not divide; whether they speak of a bag not burst, a treasury defying gravity, or a physics of evaporation and condensation, they read the verse as one testimony that the whole economy of rain, so common and so easily overlooked, is held every moment in the hand of God.
9:
The clouds that carry the rain also veil the throne of God, for he holdeth back the face of his throne, and spreadeth his cloud upon it. The reformed John Gill takes the throne to be the heaven of heavens, and the face of it the starry and airy heavens that lie before it; and this face is sometimes so held back and curtained with cloud that not even the outward appearance of the throne is to be seen. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the veiling as a mercy to weak eyes: God holds his glory back from our view, that its brightness may not dazzle us, and covers it with a cloud, for the throne is the heaven of heavens where he dwells.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the concealment a lesson in the life of faith. God conceals the glory of the upper world, holds back the dazzling face of his throne, the light in which he dwells, and spreads a cloud upon it, because he will have us live by faith and not by sight, as befits a state of probation; it would be no fair trial, Henry says, if the face of God's throne were as visible now as it will be in the great day. The grammatical-historical witnesses attend to the wording. Keil and Delitzsch note that the verb rendered "holdeth back" properly means to take hold of, even, in building, to fasten together by beams, so that God as it were closes over the face of his throne; and Charles Ellicott renders the whole "he covereth the face of his throne in the heavens, spreading his rack of cloud upon it."

Adam Clarke, another wesleyan-arminian voice, draws out the reverent inference the others leave unspoken: through all these elegant effects of an omniscient and almighty power the great Agent himself is nowhere personally discoverable, for he dwells in light unapproachable and in mercy hides himself from the view of his creatures. Or the words may be taken more simply, Clarke allows, of those darkenings of the face of heaven and the hiding of the body of the sun when the atmosphere is laden with dense vapours and the rain begins to fall. The witnesses do not divide; whether they think of the thick sky before a storm or of the eternal glory too bright for mortal sight, they agree that the same clouds which water the earth are also the merciful screen God draws before a majesty no creature could yet bear to see.
10:
Job turns from the waters above to the waters below, where God hath compassed the waters with bounds, until the day and night come to an end. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads it as the sea held in check: God sets bounds to the raging waters and compasses them in, that they may not return to cover the earth, and those bounds continue unmoved and unworn until day and night themselves come to an end and time shall be no more. Here, Henry says, is both the dominion Providence holds over the sea, as in Jer. 5:22, and its tender care of the poor sinful inhabitants of the earth, preserved from being overwhelmed as they once were by the waters of the flood.

The grammatical-historical witnesses read the "bound" as a great circle. Charles Ellicott renders the line "he hath described a circle upon the face of the waters, unto the confines of light and darkness" — the phenomenon, he explains, of the horizon at sea, which is a perfect circle and is the apparent limit of light, beyond which all is darkness and invisible. Keil and Delitzsch take it the same way: God has marked out a fixed law, a bound, over the surface of the waters unto the extreme point where the light is touched by the darkness, describing a circle that defines the sea's whole circuit.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke offers the same circle of the horizon, the line that terminates light and commences darkness — "until the completion of light with darkness" — and wonders whether the word may even carry the sky-blue tint of the horizon at twilight, where the one is ending and the other beginning; or else, more plainly, that God so circumscribes the waters, retaining them in their place, that they shall not overflow the earth until day and night, that is, time itself, come to an end. The reformed John Gill weighs whether the waters meant are those above the firmament, as the Targum inclines to take them, or the seas below, and leans away from the higher sense toward the bounded oceans of the lower world. The witnesses do not divide; whether they see the fixed shore or the circling rim of the horizon, they read the verse as one more proof that the unruly sea keeps, by God's decree, a boundary it cannot pass until the world's last day.
11:
"The pillars of heaven tremble and are astonished at his reproof" — and the witnesses agree that the pillars are the mountains, though they differ over the rebuke that shakes them. The reformed John Gill offers two candidates for the trembling columns: either the air, the lower firmament that seems to bear up the sky and is called "the firmament of his power," which quivers at thunder and lightning; or, more likely, the mountains, which reach so high that they look like the very pillars and foundations of heaven, and are indeed spoken of as its foundations, moving and shaking and trembling at the presence and power of God, and at any expression of his wrath and anger, particularly through earthquakes and storms and tempests of thunder and lightning. John Wesley, of the wesleyan-arminian school, agrees that the pillars are the mountains, which by their height and strength seem to reach and support the heavens; and he reads the "reproof" finely — they are astonished when God rebukes not them but men by them, manifesting his displeasure through thunders and earthquakes.

Adam Clarke takes the verse for a poetical description of thunder or of an earthquake — "He shakes creation with his nod; earth, sea, and heaven, confess him God" — and traces the image to the old belief that the high mountains were the pillars on which the heavens rested, the belief that made Mount Atlas a man bearing the sky upon his shoulders. He quotes Silius Italicus on Atlas propping the heavens, his cloud-girt head holding up the stars, his hoary beard white with frost and the winds roaring about his temples, to show how naturally the ancients read the mountains as the props of the firmament.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott says simply that the phenomenon of storm and tempest is in view, while Keil and Delitzsch fix the words: the towering mountains that seem to support the vault of the sky are the "pillars of heaven," the verb "tremble" denotes a violent motion back and forth, and the "reproof" is the divine command that looses or binds the powers of nature, at which the pillars stand astonished. The witnesses do not divide; they hear in the shuddering of the everlasting hills the response of the whole creation to a single word of rebuke from its Maker — the mountains themselves, that seem the very foundations of the sky, quaking like startled things at the voice of God.
12:
The hymn reaches the sea and its monster: God divideth the sea with his power, and by his understanding he smiteth through the proud. The reformed John Gill offers a wide choice of senses for the dividing — the primeval separation of the waters from the dry land, or the parting of the one sea into the many seas and channels that serve the commerce of the nations, or the cleaving of the Red Sea for Israel to pass, or the parting of the waves by a stormy wind that lifts them on high and dashes them one against another, wrinkling and furrowing them, as Jarchi read it. On "the proud" — in the Hebrew, Rahab — the debate turns, and it is a debate about the age of the book itself. Adam Clarke, of the wesleyan-arminian school, finds here a manifest allusion to the passage of the Red Sea and the overthrow of Pharaoh, since Rahab is the very name by which Egypt is called in Isa. 51:9; and he cites Calmet, that were we not prepossessed with the opinion that Job died before Moses, everyone would at first sight read the verse of that deliverance. Clarke presses the point to a conclusion: the more he studies the book, the more he is satisfied it was written long after Moses, not earlier than the days of Solomon.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott weighs the same word with more caution. The verb "divideth," he notes, is taken in the two opposite senses of stirring up and of calming, the latter perhaps fitter to a passage about God's mastery over nature; and "the proud" is literally Rahab, which certainly is at times a name for Egypt, so that, if it be so used here, it can only refer to the signal judgments at the Exodus — and by our view of that, he adds, will be settled the indication it gives of the date of Job. Keil and Delitzsch keep the plain rendering, that God rouses the sea by his power and breaks the proud one in pieces by his understanding.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry holds both readings at once. By mighty storms and tempests God divides the sea and smites through its proud waves, so that a storm furrows the waters and a calm smites them flat again, as in Ps. 89:9-10; and those who think Job lived at or after the time of Moses may apply the words to the dividing of the Red Sea and the drowning of the Egyptians, for Rahab is often put for Egypt. The witnesses do not finally agree whether the proud one smitten is the raging sea, the mythic deep, or historic Egypt at the Red Sea; but they agree that the same power which parts the waters shatters whatever lifts itself up against God.
13:
Job lifts his praise back to the heavens God has adorned: by his spirit he hath garnished the heavens; his hand hath formed the crooked serpent. The reformed John Gill reads the garnishing broadly — the visible heavens studded and bespangled with sun, moon, and stars; the invisible heavens peopled with angels and glorified saints; and the church below, the heaven on earth, garnished with the gifts and graces of the Spirit in her ministers. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the same note more warmly: by his Spirit, the eternal Spirit that moved upon the face of the waters, the breath of his mouth in Ps. 33:6, God has not merely made the heavens but beautified them, bespangling them with stars by night and painting them with the light of the sun by day, that man, made to look upward, might be led to admire the great Creator.

But "the crooked serpent" fairly divides the witnesses. Henry owns that its meaning is uncertain, and lists the guesses: the Milky Way, or some particular constellation, or — since the word is the same used for leviathan in Isa. 27:1 — the whale or the crocodile, in which the Creator's power appears. Charles Ellicott, of the grammatical-historical school, takes it for the forked lightning-flash darting across the sky like a flying serpent, though he allows that others understand the constellation of the Northern Dragon, to whose influence storms were anciently ascribed; Keil and Delitzsch render the parallel line "his hand hath formed the fugitive dragon."

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lays out the whole spread of opinion and refuses to settle it dogmatically. The garnishing he takes of the wind that sweeps and clears the sky after a storm; the crooked serpent he canvasses as the sun's serpentine path through the zodiac, or the zigzag lightning discharged from cloud to cloud, or the great sea-monsters and leviathan of creation as Calmet held, or — with Bishop Sherlock — the author of evil himself, God asserting his power over the very serpent of the fall against the two-principled creed of the sabaeans, a reading the Septuagint supports with its "by a decree he destroyed the apostate dragon." From so many contradictory opinions Clarke draws his standing rule, that no metaphor or figurative expression should ever be pressed as the proof of an article of faith. The witnesses do not divide over the glory of the adorned heavens; they divide only over the serpent traced across them — lightning, constellation, sea-monster, or the tempter overmastered by his Maker.
14:
"Lo, these are parts of his ways: but how little a portion is heard of him? but the thunder of his power who can understand?" — Job seals the hymn with an awe that dwarfs everything he has said. The reformed John Gill reads "parts" as the extremities, the edges and borders and outlines of God's ways; so far is Job from thinking he has traced the chief of them that he calls all he has named the mere fringe, and asks, if these outlines are so marvellous, what must the whole be that lies beyond the reach of man to describe? The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley says the same: these are but small parcels, the outside and visible work, a portion only of God's power and wisdom and providence; and that power is aptly likened to thunder, for its irresistible force and the terror it strikes into wicked men.

The grammatical-historical witnesses fasten on the contrast of the whisper and the thunder. Adam Clarke, another wesleyan-arminian voice, notes that "parts" is ketsoth, the ends or extremities, an indistinct sketch, while "how little a portion is heard" is shemets, a mere whisper, admirably opposed, as Mr. Good observed, to the raam, the thunder, of the next clause: as a whisper is to thunder, so are the infinitely varied works of God to the faint outline Job has drawn. Keil and Delitzsch confirm the reading, taking the word for the extremest end-points of God's ways and hearing in the "whisper" only the faintest breath of a might that fills the whole creation and transcends all understanding. Charles Ellicott renders "how little a portion is heard" as "how little do we hear," and "the thunder of his power" as the thunder of his mighty deeds: we catch but the faintest whisper of his glory, and can neither comprehend nor endure the full-toned thunder of his majesty.

Ellicott draws out what the verse means for the whole dispute. This is Job's final reply, and in it he shows himself even more conscious than his friends of the grandeur and holiness of God; yet that grandeur has made his own case as a sufferer no more intelligible, and theirs, as defenders of an exact retribution, no more defensible: he cannot understand, and they cannot explain, and while he rejects their explanations he rests secure in his own faith. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lands where Paul does, despairing to find the bottom and sitting down at the brink to adore the depth — "O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God!" in Rom. 11:33 — for what we know of God is nothing to what is in God, and even the thunder of his power, one of the lowest of his ways, we cannot understand. The witnesses do not divide; they close the chapter bowed together before a majesty of which they have heard only a whisper.
